result.white_space:
Nobody I found sells a US, insurer-facing, explainable edit library (canonical line-item codes, bundling and duplicate rules, unit plausibility, reason codes) with cross-carrier benchmarks, to mid-size MGAs and TPAs.

- VetControl is the only true direct analog, and it is German, GOT-based, a services-plus-software hybrid, and shows no US customers.
- Five Sigma and Sirma classify line items for coverage, not for pricing or bundling.
- FairVet and Vet Receipt hold consumer-sourced benchmark data with no insurer-grade normalization.
- Trupanion and Lassie built in-house and are not customers.
- Verisk has standardized the policy side only.

The unserved gap is an invoice-derived, ZIP-level, procedure-level price index built from insurer claims, which no owner-upload app can match in volume. It would be joined to explainable pay/reduce/review decisions for mid-size carriers with no data science team.

Structural risk to flag. Human-health edits work because of provider contracts and CMS rules. Pet insurers have no contracts with vets and no 'global fee' concept, and they pay owners by reimbursement. Line-level reductions therefore land on policyholders as balance bills, which invites complaints and regulatory attention. I found no US insurer RFP or public spend for this. The demand evidence is indirect: cost inflation, plus vendors like VetControl selling a similar product in Germany.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Indirect but real; no direct US RFP or disclosed spend found.

1. Severity pressure. The UK CMA's final report (24 Mar 2026) found vet prices up 63% and first-year treatment costs up 53% from 2016 to 2023, against 32% general services inflation. Consolidated practices show about 5% higher claim values and 9.2% higher prices within four years. Sources: https://www.abi.org.uk/news/blog-articles/2026/6/cma-veterinary-services-report-pet-insurance/ and https://www.insurancetimes.co.uk/analysis/has-corporate-consolidation-broken-the-pet-insurance-model/1458814.article. The US BLS figure of veterinary services up 4.7% year on year to Jul 2026 is cited at https://fairvethq.com/blog/vet-care-inflation-2026. Trupanion's FY2025 10-K also says vet care costs are outpacing inflation: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1371285/000137128526000018/trup-20251231.htm.
2. Regulation creating standardized inputs. The CMA order (deadline 23 Sep 2026) phases in standard price lists for common services, itemised billing and written estimates above 500 GBP over 3 to 12 months (https://www.wisepet.co.uk/guides/cma-vet-reforms/). That gives UK insurers a de facto canonical procedure list to match against.
3. Insurers already pay for line-item work. Sirma built PetsBest a line-item classifier and reports a 300% productivity gain (https://sirma.com/use-cases/sirma-s-ai-driven-solution-is-transforming-claims-processing-and-enhancing-efficiency-for-u-s-insurer.html). Five Sigma reports 90% shorter cycle times at a US pet insurer (https://fivesigmalabs.com/blog/five-sigma-clive-ai-pet-insurance-claims-stp-90-percent-faster/). VetControl sells invoice verification to insurers and claims 'up to 25%' lower payouts (https://vetcontrol.team/en-us/index.html).
4. Consumer-side price transparency is being funded and crowd-sourced (FairVet claims 3M bills, https://fairvethq.com/; Vet Receipt, https://vetreceipt.com/), which shows the data has value.
5. The lack of codes is widely acknowledged. Vet PMS terminology is inconsistent, VeNom has about 800 procedure codes (https://venomcoding.org/venom-codes/), and SNOMED CT is not widely adopted in vet practice (https://priorknowledgeandpractice.substack.com/p/why-veterinary-medicine-needs-standardized).

Caveat: many 'demand' pages (Insurnest and similar blogs) are SEO content, not evidence. The WebSearch budget hit its 200-call session cap, so I could not run further Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt sweeps. I found no pet-specific edit product from a funded US startup, but that is not proof none exists.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not lead with 'unbundling edits'. Without provider contracts, they push cost onto owners and will draw pushback. Lead with a cross-carrier claims data utility:

1. Wedge (paid now). Map free-text vet lines to VeNom or SNOMED-VET codes and to each carrier's coverage categories, with explainable reason codes. This is what Sirma and Five Sigma prove insurers pay for, and it lets you ingest 100k-2M claims per MGA without being an adjudication platform.
2. Moat (network effect). Mid-size MGAs and TPAs contribute anonymized line-level invoices in exchange for a pooled, ZIP and practice-type price index, in the Verisk ISO consortium model. No single insurer (Trupanion, Lassie) or owner-upload app (FairVet, Vet Receipt, roughly 3M or 2.9k bills) can match its depth for mid-size carriers.
3. Turn edits into advisory flags and pre-service tools instead of retroactive cuts. Examples are pre-treatment estimate checks at direct-pay checkout, and provider-facing feedback that shows outlier lines before submission.
4. Sell the consolidator angle. Track pricing and claim-value drift by corporate group versus independents (the CMA found about 5% higher claim values after takeover). This gives insurers negotiating data for direct-pay networks and reference pricing, which no competitor found offers.
5. Sequence: the US mid-market first, then the UK. CMA-mandated itemised bills and standard price lists from late 2026 give UK insurers a ready canonical list, and consolidators there have strong pricing power.
6. Validate the risk first. Ask 10 MGAs for their policy language on usual and customary limits and their balance-bill complaint rates, and confirm that line-level reductions are actually permissible before building the edit layer.

result.white_space:
Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. The fight is over how many samples, where, and against what background, and no independent tool scores a sampling plan or existing IH report for adequacy, though this is what class actions and the Purdue review turn on. (3) A neutral, versioned crosswalk from AIHA/IICRC/40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels and 8 CCR 1529 asbestos to a per-home plan, which updates when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. (4) Pooled, structured sampling data across claims, which is what regulators reuse. EFRU holds only a few dozen homes.

Two facts weaken the 'vacuum' framing. Interim lead and asbestos thresholds already exist in AB 1642 (40 CFR 745.227(e)(8)(viii) and 8 CCR 1529). The vacuum is mainly sampling design and non-lead contaminants such as cyanide, other metals and dioxins.

Structural risks: the buyer conflict, because carriers may not adopt a protocol seen as policyholder-friendly and policyholder-side buyers want a testifying CIH rather than software. Remote IH sign-off and technician-collected samples may run into CIH and certification expectations. Any advantage is capped at the moment DTSC publishes standards.

Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Demand is strong and forced by law, but the paying buyer is not the one the idea assumes.

Statute: AB 1795 (signed 9/15/2026, effective 1/1/2027) makes insurers inspect within 30 days and pay for sampling and testing needed to restore homes to pre-loss condition and clear them for occupancy (Sec. 2060.2(b), (d)(1)). It sets a rebuttable presumption that smoke, ash, soot and char in a surviving home in the impact zone came from the fire, and bars ALE termination before clearance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB1795 ; https://www.insurancebusinessmag.com/us/news/property/california-sets-first-wildfire-smoke-testing-rules-for-insurers-588314.aspx). DTSC standards are due end-2028 (lead and asbestos) and end-2029 (other contaminants) (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1642 ; https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/california-los-angeles-palisades-eaton-fires-smoke-damage-bills-signed-wildfire-insurance). CalMatters/Pleasanton Weekly describe a gap of about 2+ years (https://www.pleasantonweekly.com/calmatters/2026/09/15/new-california-law-sets-first-in-nation-standards-for-smoke-damage-in-homes/).

Volume: coverage of the CDI task force cites more than 42,000 LA-fire claims from Jan-Nov 2025, over 13,000 of them standing homes with smoke damage. I could not pin the exact source. CDI task force report (3/9/2026): https://www.insurance.ca.gov/01-consumers/140-catastrophes/Smoke-Claims-Remediation-Report.cfm

Litigation over sampling design: Ghazarian v. Fire Insurance Exchange and HygieneTech class action (https://pasadenanow.com/main/altadena-homeowners-sue-farmers-insurance-testing-firm-over-eaton-fire-smoke-claims); a second class action against a carrier and its hygiene vendor (https://www.law.com/therecorder/2026/02/27/hygiene-companies-face-class-actions-over-alleged-failure-to-properly-test-homes-for-toxins-after-eaton-wildfire-/); LA County suit vs State Farm, 8/31/2026 (https://www.liveinsurancenews.com/smoke-damage-claims-california/8575801/).

The problem the idea names, thin sampling: carrier-retained hygienists take about ten samples in a 3,000 sq ft home (1 per 300 sq ft), skip wall cavities, attic insulation and HVAC unless the homeowner pays, and cap budgets in advance (https://www.propertyinsurancecoveragelaw.com/blog/california-wildfire-smoke-claims/). Purdue reports consultants using improper methods and incorrect comparison standards (https://engineering.purdue.edu/PlumbingSafety/resources/wildfire-response).

Willingness to pay: independent testing runs $2,000-$20,000+ (https://www.kerleyschaffer.com/blog/fair-plan-hygenist-testing-guide). Homeowners already pay about $2k-$4k out of pocket, which supports the $1,800-$4,500 price point. EFRU's data on about 50 remediated homes showed 63% with elevated lead and one third with asbestos (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/altadena-eaton-fire-homes-post-remediation-testing-lead-asbestos).

Not found: any carrier, TPA or RFP saying it wants to buy a third-party protocol or compliance dashboard. Carriers oppose the bills and retain their own vendors (https://calmatters.org/economy/2026/09/smoke-damage-insurance-bills/). The claimed $2-$5 per claim per month SaaS demand is unvalidated.
result.sharper_angle:
Drop 'write the standard' and the 'training and certification' revenue line. Build the AB 1795 defensibility and compliance layer as a capital-light, software-first product.

1. Sell a sampling-plan generator and adequacy auditor to carriers, TPAs and litigation-side buyers. The plan generator sets zone-aware sample counts and locations, including attics, HVAC and wall cavities, and picks the comparison basis: EPA 40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels, 8 CCR 1529 asbestos, and pre-/post-remediation and background controls. Every plan cites AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI and Purdue and is versioned so it re-maps when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. The auditor scores any existing IH report against the same grid, which is the exact issue in the HygieneTech and State Farm actions. That serves the 'fight is the sampling design' insight without a technician army.

2. Use existing CIH and IICRC firms as the labor pool and operate as the compliance and evidence layer: 30-day clock, chain-of-custody, lab results, audit trail. Rimkus, EHS, Safeguard and similar firms are then partners or channel, not enemies. Sign remote CIH-of-record through partner firms rather than hiring your own, to avoid licensure and certification exposure.

3. Take a neutral-standards posture: an advisory board of CIHs plus a toxicologist, public methodology, and an anonymized cross-claim dataset. Aim to be the data source DTSC and CDI can cite. Try to get pilot data-sharing with EFRU and Purdue instead of competing with their free guides.

4. Start with the buyers who feel the pain and can be reached before 1/1/2027, and validate before building. The first test is whether one carrier or TPA claims team will pay for a paid pilot on 10-20 files. Public adjusters and policyholder attorneys are the fastest early revenue (expert-evidence sampling plans and report audits). Use the subsidized pilot assessments only as data collection. If no carrier or TPA will sign, the fallback is a PA and attorney tool.

5. Position for the next fire. AB 1795 covers any declared wildfire, and other states (CO, OR, HI) will copy California. A product that re-maps to whichever standard governs is more durable than a California-specific interim protocol that dies in 2028.

Before committing, verify the chaptered AB 1795 text on three points: interim local-agency standards, the state training and certification programs, and any qualified-person requirements for samplers. One source (Insurance Business) says DTSC emergency regulations are due 7/1/2027 and that AIHA and IICRC guides 'carry statutory force'. CalMatters, LAist and the AB 1642 text say end-2028 and end-2029, and I did not find the statutory-force claim in the bill text I could read.

What looks unserved, and is specific: (1) a contingency service focused only on the implant/device carve-out. It would join the OR implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers) to the AP vendor invoice, then to the payer contract carve-out clause, then to the 835 line. None of the general underpayment vendors above advertise this. (2) The buyer is the physician-owned spine/ortho ASC. Enterprise tools like Sift, FinThrive and Aspirion are aimed at health systems. (3) The claim-side fix is assembling the invoice attachment per payer rules and filing a corrected claim inside timely-filing limits. General contract-modeling tools mostly stop at flagging a variance.

Risks to the premise:
- 'Nobody connects them' is overstated. Becker's ran 'ASC Implant Carve-Outs: Opportunities, Challenges & 4 Best Practices' in 2014, so ASC operators know carve-outs exist (https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-coding-billing-and-collections/asc-implant-carve-outs-opportunities-challenges-4-best-practices/). ASC-specialist billers such as SIS/Surgical Notes, National Medical Billing Services and Nimble probably submit implant invoices as routine, so the addressable leakage may sit mostly in ASCs with weak or outsourced generalist billing.
- Any player with a contingency model and payer-contract modeling could add this quickly. Aspirion's ContractIQ is the most obvious.
- Medicare does not carve out implants in the ASC setting, so this is a commercial-contract play only. Each payer contract must be read individually, which limits how far it scales.
- I could not verify the CY2026 IPO-list phase-out and ASC list additions cited in the idea's why-now. CMS's page confirms only that a CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) exists.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Indirect only. I found no direct evidence (forum complaints, RFPs or pricing pages) that ASCs pay a third party to recover unbilled implant carve-outs.

Supportive signals from Becker's ASC, snippets only because the article bodies returned 403:
- 'ASCs' implant cost problem' (Mar 12, 2026): 'For many ASCs, implants have become a difficult expense to manage, often requiring large upfront payments while reimbursement remains inconsistent.' https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-coding-billing-and-collections/ascs-implant-cost-problem/
- 'The burden of implant costs: 10 things ASCs need to know' (Feb 12, 2025): 'High costs of surgical implants have been identified as a profitability-killer for ASCs.' https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-coding-billing-and-collections/the-burden-of-implant-costs-10-things-ascs-need-to-know/
- 'The payer terms ASCs can't miss' (Jul 2026): 'payer talks this year came down to fine print, implant costs and case-level cost data.' https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-coding-billing-and-collections/the-payer-terms-ascs-cant-miss/
- Nimble Solutions sponsored content: 'ASCs face heightened revenue and cash flow risk... particularly with implant-and device heavy procedures.' https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-transactions-and-valuation-issues/unlocking-cash-flow-3-proven-ar-strategies-every-asc-needs/
- Becker's search for 'implant carve-out' returns 219 results and 'implant billing vendor' returns 187, so the topic is heavily covered.

There is also existing spend on adjacent contingency recovery: Aspirion reports $6B+ in client recoveries and sells on a contingency model (https://www.aspirion.com). That shows buyers accept contingency recovery in general, not for this niche.

The other demand evidence, that unbilled carve-outs are large and invisible, comes only from the idea file and is unverified. It needs the free 90-day lookback audits to prove.
result.sharper_angle:
Don't pitch 'revenue cycle recovery'. Pitch a narrow implant-to-cash reconciliation for spine and ortho ASCs, sold as a contingency lookback that turns into a prospective pre-bill check.

1. Start with the join no one else does: OR implant log (lot and catalog numbers) to vendor invoice to payer carve-out clause to 835 line. Compute an expected carve-out payment per case, at invoice cost plus the contract's markup.
2. Run the first 5-10 audits by hand with a coder, on payers whose contracts explicitly carve out implants. That yields a real dollar figure per case as sales proof.
3. Sell it to the ASC's surgeon-owners and administrator, not to health-system finance, since that is where the enterprise tools don't sell. Go through ASCA chapters and ASC management companies.
4. Make the durable product a pre-bill gate. Before the claim goes out, it checks that the invoice is attached and that the L8699 or 027x line is coded to trigger the carve-out. Contingency recovery is the wedge and prospective monitoring is the recurring revenue.
5. Build channel deals with the ASC billing vendors and ASC software vendors (SIS, HST, Nimble). Offer them a white-label carve-out audit rather than competing head-on.

Before building, run the 3-5 free lookbacks to test whether the leakage is real. If ASC-specialist billers already capture most carve-outs, the market shrinks to poorly billed ASCs and small hospitals. Then re-run the competitor check with live WebSearch (Cloudmed/R1, Experian, small implant-billing consultancies, YC and Crunchbase), which this pass could not do.

result.white_space: The unserved wedge is narrow. It is vendor-neutral, rack-level verification of the manifold and quick-disconnect layer after the facility loops are flushed, sold to neocloud owners, lenders and insurers who want independent proof. What I found does not cover it: PurgeRite covers facility and loop flushing, ChemTreat covers cleaning and chemistry, and OEMs cover the CDU and rack they sold. None of the fetched pages mention per-quick-disconnect photo, QR and serial records, re-test after thermal cycling, or an independent inspector-of-record. A second gap is small and mid-size neocloud and colo builds outside hyperscaler purchasing. Crews for hire is not white space: flushing, purging and pre-operational cleaning are already owned by funded consolidators (Vertiv/PurgeRite, Ecolab/CoolIT, Trane/LiquidStack, ChemTreat/Dow), and mechanical contractors and OEMs can quietly absorb pressure-testing. Caveat: WebSearch hit its session cap, so I did not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or other small firms. A tiny field-service specialist I missed (Compu Dynamics, Salute and similar) may already sell this.
result.evidence_of_demand: Real, but this is inferred from adjacent evidence, and I found no RFPs or forum threads. (1) Buyers are paying for liquid-loop field services. Vertiv bought PurgeRite in Dec 2025 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertiv), and PurgeRite reports 10+ hyperscale clients and 100+ data center flushes (https://www.purgerite.com/about-us/). (2) Strategic capital is flowing into cooling plus service. Ecolab bought CoolIT for $4.75B (closed 2 July 2026, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecolab), and Trane bought LiquidStack for its 'global service, deployment and lifecycle-support organization' (https://www.datacenterfrontier.com/cooling/article/55381913/liquid-cooling-market-matures-innovations-acquisitions-and-modular-solutions-for-ai-infrastructure). (3) Viega's sponsored DCF article states that 'certified pipe welders and specialized fitters are increasingly difficult to source' and that 'late-stage leaks discovered during system charging are catastrophic' (https://www.datacenterfrontier.com/sponsored/article/55400568/installing-cooling-that-scales-why-pipe-joining-speed-and-integrity-are-the-bottlenecks-in-ai-infrastructure). That article gives no dollar figures. (4) ChemTreat sells pre-operational cleaning for TCS loops (https://www.chemtreat.com/data-centers/). Not verified: the idea's $14M per month commissioning-delay figure and the July 2026 survey.
result.sharper_angle: Drop the 'crew of plumbers' framing, because that is what Vertiv/PurgeRite, ChemTreat/Dow and the mechanical contractors already sell and finance. Sell independent third-party rack-level wet-work assurance instead. An inspector-of-record team, small and skilled, arrives after the mechanical contractor and the flushing vendor. It pressure-decay tests and borescopes every manifold and quick-disconnect pair and logs each one to a rack serial, QR tag and photo in a lender- and insurer-ready package. It then returns after thermal cycling (30, 90 and 180 days) for re-verification. Price it per rack plus a subscription to the record and a re-inspect option. Because it is independent, it does not compete with the flush vendors. It can also subcontract to them and to the mechanical contractors, who need cover for the rack layer. Start with neocloud and GPU-lender projects (GPU-backed debt draws create a demand for proof) in one metro. Before building, confirm with 5 to 10 owners that they will pay for the assurance layer and not just for labor. Also run the searches I could not: Crunchbase/YC, Compu Dynamics, Salute, and the OCP commissioning guidelines.

result.white_space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. Three structural weaknesses limit the wedge. (a) The clocks mostly start at OEM startup, and startup plus IST with load banks already loads equipment in Cx, so the 'idle for 12+ months' exposure is narrower than the pitch implies. It mainly hits gear started early or shipped more than 18 months before use. (b) 'Recovered value' is really avoided repair cost. It is hard to measure and easy for OEMs to dispute, and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds (wet stacking is explicitly excluded, https://cliffordpower.com/wet-stacking-why-its-important-to-load-bank-your-diesel-generator/). A pure 25-30% contingency model will be hard to collect. (c) Documents are the commodity step, so the moat has to be inspection plus OEM leverage, not the LLM pipeline.
result.evidence_of_demand: Indirect only. I found no direct customer complaints, RFPs, or forum threads saying a hall's warranty lapsed while idle. Supporting evidence, weakest to strongest: (1) OEM terms create the shipment-based outer limit: Cummins (18 months from ship) https://www.cummins.com/sites/default/files/2018-08/A042E778.pdf, Eaton (18 months from ship) https://www.eaton.com/us/en/catalog/services/startup--warranty-and-support-overview/eaton-93e-ups-startup--warranty-and-support-overview.html, Trane (12 months from startup or 18 from ship, with a paid delayed-start rider) https://www.trane.com/commercial/north-america/us/en/services/operate-maintain-repair/hvac-system-management/extended-warranty.html. That OEMs sell a delayed-start rider shows the problem is real and priced. (2) Law firm guidance tells developers to make contractor warranties commence no earlier than Tier Certification, which shows owners think about warranty timing: https://www.womblebonddickinson.com/us/insights/alerts/critical-performance-guarantees-data-center-construction-contracts-and-risk. (3) Data center Cx firms already sell a 10-month pre-expiry warranty review, so owners pay for this kind of service: https://www.ethyco.com/services.html. (4) Wind energy shows a mature paid market for end-of-warranty inspections, because OEMs reject claims filed after expiry: https://www.sgs.com/en-us/services/end-of-warranty-inspection and https://skyspecs.com/blog/end-of-warranty-inspections/. (5) Fleet warranty recovery is a known leak: spreadsheet tracking recovers only ~15-22% of owed warranty value (https://fleetrabbit.com/industry/construction-management-system/construction-equipment-warranty-tracking-oem-claims), and outsourced warranty administration is an established business (https://www.warrantyconsultants.com/). (6) Idle-capital cost is large: $15-40M financing charges on a $500M build sitting idle (https://exto360.com/the-30-150m-problem-why-commissioning-delays-are-the-biggest-risk-in-data-center-construction/), which makes owners attentive but is a schedule pain, not a warranty pain. The 'why now' premise is contested. Reports say ~half of 2026 US capacity is not under construction (https://www.theregister.com/on-prem/2026/06/17/only-half-of-us-datacenter-capacity-planned-for-2026-is-actually-under-construction/5257781), but SemiAnalysis argues most of that is phantom announcements and shows no evidence of energized-but-empty halls (https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/stop-saying-half-of-2026-us-datacenter). The target population of 'commissioned 6-14 months ago and unloaded' is unproven and must be validated with real owners.
result.sharper_angle: Drop the generic 'warranty recovery audit' and the 25-30% contingency lead. Position it as an end-of-warranty load-test sprint for energized-but-underloaded halls, the wind end-of-warranty inspection model ported to data center MEP. Product: 6-9 months before each OEM clock expires, rent load banks (Aggreko/Sunbelt-type partners) and use the hall's idle capacity to run staged loaded tests on gensets (avoiding wet-stacking exclusions), UPS/battery, chillers/CDUs and breakers while the OEM is still liable. Then file claims with OEM-grade evidence and negotiate deferral or extension riders (Trane-style delayed-start warranty). Lead with a fixed-fee audit ($15-40K) and add a success fee only on defects the test actually surfaces. Sell to whoever needs certainty on a dated event: the owner's lender or technical advisor, ABS or refinancing due diligence, and buyers of stabilized powered-shell assets. Put the document-extraction pipeline behind the scenes as an internal tool, since Anyset, Nomic and Equipment Warranty Log are commoditizing it. Partner with, or pre-empt, Cx firms like Ethyco rather than compete with them, and add a PO-stage clause pack plus deferred-start rider brokerage as a cheap top-of-funnel. Before building, do the one check the research could not complete: find 5-10 owners with halls actually energized and idle 8-14 months, and confirm from their OEM terms and startup dates that clocks are running out on unloaded equipment.

result.white_space:
A real gap remains, but it is much narrower than the pitch. Nobody found sells a commercial-lines, broker-facing workflow that (1) takes a book's actual renewal forms schedules, quotes and binders (not just carrier-level filings), (2) detects and normalises AI exclusion breadth for each client, including bespoke wording such as Berkley PC 51380 and unnamed 'AI' language, (3) ties it to a 90-day renewal calendar, and (4) hands the producer a client-ready gap letter and a matched affirmative placement. Pieces exist separately. Patra reads commercial policies for hidden exclusions but is not AI-specific. Quandri and Zywave own the 90-day renewal trigger but show no exclusion-level AI flagging. Testudo and Armilla offer AI-use mapping and placement but only for their own paper.

Three parts of the plan are weak. (a) The SERFF scraper and exclusion database are not a moat. Trades Coverage already compiled 4,078 records for free. Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs and ShadowLock publish free trackers, and Certian even ships CC BY 4.0 CSV and JSON. (b) A filing shows a carrier adopted a form in a state. It does not show the form is attached to client X's policy, so the real signal is the policy document, not the filing. (c) SERFF filing access covers admitted markets only. Surplus lines is where most E&O, D&O and tech-E&O AI exclusions sit, and it is largely invisible to SERFF.

Wedge that looks unserved: commercial professional-liability and tech-E&O accounts (design firms, law, accounting, software, agencies) where exclusions are broadest and most bespoke, for independent agencies without an in-house risk-advisory team, priced as a renewal-review add-on rather than a filings database.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Strong evidence that the problem is real and urgent. Direct evidence that brokers pay for this specific tool is thin.

Problem and urgency:
- ISO CG 40 47, CG 40 48 and CG 35 08 took effect 1 Jan 2026, and W. R. Berkley introduced an 'absolute' AI exclusion for D&O, E&O and fiduciary lines (https://natlawreview.com/article/continued-proliferation-ai-exclusions).
- Trades Coverage counted 4,078 state-level filing records across 49 states plus DC, with 2,369 in force by 31 July 2026 (https://www.insurancebusinessmag.com/us/news/professional-liability/isos-generative-ai-exclusion-is-already-on-thousands-of-cgl-policies-589971.aspx). Substack coverage reports Berkshire, Chubb, Travelers and AIG got over 80% of filings approved, with Florida, Connecticut and Maryland leading volume (https://insuranceintel.substack.com/p/berkshire-and-chubb-just-won-approval).
- Exclusions arrive silently: the renewal invoice can be almost identical while the policy is materially different, because an exclusion endorsement usually does not change the premium (https://techsavvyinsurance.com/blog/ai-eo-exclusion-insurance-agents-2026/).
- The Independent Insurance Agents & Brokers of America ('Big I') published the Verisk rollout as a resource for agents (https://www.independentagent.com/vu_resource/verisk-to-roll-out-new-general-liability-exclusions-for-generative-ai-exposures/). Agent-association and trade content now urges agents to review renewals for AI exclusions (https://agentsunited.org/ai-exclusions-are-coming/, https://www.iamagazine.com/2026/09/09/5-ways-insurance-agencies-can-reduce-ai-driven-eo-exposures/).
- Gallagher says it is 'watching this very closely' because gaps may emerge (https://www.businessinsurance.com/insurers-brokers-adjust-as-ai-exclusions-emerge/).

Willingness to pay for adjacent tooling:
- Quandri raised about US$22M and has 100+ agencies paying for renewal policy checking (https://betakit.com/quandri-secures-16-5-million-cad-to-help-north-american-insurance-firms-automate-renewals-with-ai/).
- Zywave launched a renewal and coverage-gap agent for the 90-day window (https://www.zywave.com/ai/advisor-agent/).
- Patra sells commercial policy checking that flags hidden exclusions (https://www.patracorp.com/insurance-outsourcing-services/insurance-policy-checking-ai/).
- Rosella raised A$3.7M on policy comparison that surfaces exclusions (https://www.startupdaily.net/topic/funding/ai-insurance-broker-platform-rosella-raises-3-7-million-in-pre-seed/).
- Affirmative AI capacity is being built for the placement half: Testudo, Armilla, AIUC and Munich Re aiSure (https://www.testudo.co/brokers, https://medium.com/@purdyhouse/the-first-ai-liability-insurance-product-has-25-million-in-coverage-five-exist-worldwide-575a2903b17b).

Caveats:
- The founder's premise that brokers carry E&O exposure for failing to warn is weaker than stated. In most states an agent has no duty to advise on every exclusion in a policy (per the Tech Savvy Insurance article above, which reports the duty-to-advise rule as varying by state).
- I found no evidence that anyone pays for a standalone AI-exclusion tracker. Every tracker found is free and used as lead generation.
- Small business owners are largely unaware of the exclusions (business insurance blog claim: https://www.businessinsuranceusa.com/blog/insurance/ai-coverage-gap-small-business-insurance-2026/).
result.sharper_angle:
Do not lead with the SERFF scraper or exclusion database as the product or moat. Free trackers (Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs, ShadowLock) and Trades Coverage's 4,078-record dataset already commoditise it. Use the public filings only as a free enrichment and validation layer, and win on the document layer plus the workflow.

Build an 'AI exclusion diff' for commercial professional-liability renewals (E&O, D&O, cyber, tech E&O and CGL for professional-services clients, including design, law, accounting, software and marketing firms). The producer forwards the renewal quote, binder or policy PDF, and the tool returns a per-client breadth score covering: gen-AI only versus any AI, BI/PD versus advertising injury, and vendor-supplied AI. Where a carrier's exclusion is bespoke, it matches the wording against the filing library. A diff against the expiring policy shows whether an AI exclusion is new, and it ships a client-ready gap letter. Because it works from the policy document, it also covers surplus-lines paper, which SERFF does not.

Sell it per renewal ($150-600 per client gap letter) or as a small monthly plan, and design it as an add-on or partner integration for Epic and Zywave rather than a competing AMS or dashboard. Zywave's Advisor Agent and Quandri already own the 90-day trigger, and a specialist AI-exclusion classifier is a feature they may buy or copy. Make the placement side neutral: route to several affirmative markets (Testudo, Armilla, AIUC, Mount, Munich Re/Mosaic, Coalition-style endorsements) and earn referral revenue. Test the 10-15% commission assumption first, because the carriers courting brokers directly may not pay it.

Validate first with 10 agencies that have professional-services or tech books: run their real last three renewals through a manual version and measure how many contain an AI exclusion the broker had not flagged. If that hit rate is high, sell to those agencies. If most already knew, the wedge is gone."

result.white_space:
Caveat: the WebSearch budget hit its cap (200 of 200) before I could run the planned searches on startups, Crunchbase, Product Hunt and forums. This verdict rests on direct page fetches only. Treat 'gap' as provisional. Before building, someone should spend an hour on the searches I could not run: 'letter of protection medical bill review', 'reasonable value expert Florida LOP', and Crunchbase/YC for 'LOP' or 'defense medical bill'.

What I could confirm: no vendor I could reach sells a fixed-fee (about $300-700), fast-turnaround, coder-certified report with an optional declaration or testimony upsell aimed at LOP reasonable value. The nearest product is Enlyte's Demand Package Review. It is a carrier-side workflow product with nurse and analyst review at 3-4 to 10 days. It shows no coder signature, no LOP framing and no testimony. It also lacks the piece defense lawyers need most, which is a signed opinion that survives cross-examination. Data companies (FAIR Health, Turquoise) sell inputs, not signed opinions. EvenUp is plaintiff-side.

Specific white space: (1) small and mid-size defense firms and panel counsel who can't justify a $3-5k expert on a $30-100k claim. (2) Coder-signed output that holds up under cross-examination, tied to the LOP disclosure record. (3) States without a statutory benchmark, where reasonable value is contested.

Two weaknesses in the pitch. (a) Florida is partly commoditized by statute. Fla. Stat. 768.0427 (https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0768/Sections/0768.0427.html) already makes evidence of what was actually paid, or 120% of Medicare (170% of Medicaid where there is no Medicare rate), the benchmark for uninsured claimants. The fetched summary does not settle whether that applies to LOP treatment, so check the statute text. A large part of the Florida 'report' is therefore a Medicare-multiple calculation from free CMS files, which a claims shop or existing vendor could copy quickly. (b) The hospital price-transparency 'why now' is weaker than the idea claims. CMS says enforcement of the new rules starts April 1, 2026 (https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/hospital-price-transparency). But LOP care is mostly delivered by chiropractors, pain clinics, orthopedic groups and physician-owned ASCs, not hospitals. I inferred that from how LOP cases usually work and did not verify it. The defensible professional-fee benchmarks would come from Medicare multiples, payer transparency-in-coverage files or licensed data, not hospital files.

Partial evidence, all inferred from statute and vendor marketing. I found no forum complaints, RFPs or quoted willingness-to-pay for this exact product.

(1) Statute forcing the analysis. Florida 768.0427 requires claimants to disclose the LOP, itemized billing with procedure codes, any factoring company and the dollar amount it paid for the account, coverage status and who referred the treatment, and makes the law-firm/provider relationship admissible. That creates a structured record defense counsel has to analyze. Source: https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0768/Sections/0768.0427.html and the bill page https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2023/837. I could not fetch the Georgia 2025 tort-reform text (legiscan returned 403), so the Georgia and other-state claims in the idea are unverified.

(2) Carriers already pay for adjacent outsourced bill analysis. Enlyte sells Demand Package Review as a paid service, with a nurse tier and a stated '60% average reduction in medical charges' and '$5-7K improvement in average settlement' (https://www.enlyte.com/solutions/casualty/cost-containment-services/demand-package-review). Enlyte also publishes content about 'Questionable Billing Patterns' in demands (https://www.enlyte.com/insights/article/injury-liability/bodily-injury-demand-review). These figures are vendor marketing.

(3) The plaintiff-side spending arms race. EvenUp raised $150M at a $2B+ valuation (Oct 2025) to build better demands and treatment management for plaintiff firms (https://www.evenuplaw.com/newsroom). It implies defense spend is likely to follow, but it is not direct proof.

(4) The idea's own premise, that experts cost $3-5k, is unverified. None found: forum threads, RFPs, or published prices for coder-signed reports.
result.sharper_angle: Narrow it and sell it as an evidence product, not a report. (1) Start in a state without a statutory Medicare-multiple benchmark, such as Georgia, Texas or Louisiana, where reasonable value is contested and a signed local benchmark carries more weight. Treat Florida as a rebuttal-of-plaintiff-expert product, since 768.0427 already supplies a free benchmark. (2) Build the report around the LOP disclosure record. Ingest the letter, the itemized coded bill, the factoring purchase price and the referral relationship. Compute the statutory or market benchmark, flag litigation-built billing patterns, and hand counsel cross-examination questions keyed to specific lines. The factoring price and referral facts are what a generic bill-review vendor won't tie together. (3) Make the testimony the profit center. Give reports away cheaply as lead generation, and sell the declaration and testimony ($1,500-3,500) as the margin. Build a library of transcripts and Daubert outcomes as the moat. (4) Sell first to volume defense firms and panel-counsel programs, which have the acute pain and are underserved by Enlyte-style carrier workflow tools. Approach carrier vendors like Enlyte as a partner that supplies the coder signature and testimony layer, rather than competing head-on. (5) Before committing, do the searches I could not run and check whether an established expert practice already sells flat-fee LOP reasonable-value reports in Florida or Georgia.

Reposition as the evidence and service-delivery ledger, meaning the system of record for whether the district delivered what the IEP promised.

Core product: the parent enters or forwards provider session notes, missed-session emails and school-portal data. The system maps them to each IEP service line, computes minutes owed vs delivered per period, and outputs a compensatory-services claim packet with a tamper-evident timeline and dated, written requests. The AI drafting is a commodity feature. The ledger and the packet are the product.

Add a human-verified tier ($75 per 30 minutes with a vetted advocate or attorney) to answer the fabricated-citation problem CADRE and K-12 Dive flag. Wrap it in a 'reviewed before filing' step so complaints are accurate. State agencies and districts are absorbing a 56% rise in AI-drafted complaints and have a reason to welcome well-formed filings.

Go to market through parent centers, disability law clinics and credit unions at $3-6 per member per month, which IEP Advocate.ai has no B2B offer for. Start with one or two states with strong complaint processes.

I found no funded startup or incumbent selling a done-for-you, small-brand, monitored CBP program (recordation, ID guide, 24-hour authentication desk, detention monitoring, evidence packaging). That is weaker evidence than a clean search sweep, so rerun searches for customs recordation subscription services, and for the CBP offerings of Red Points, Corsearch and IP boutiques, before building. What looks unserved: (1) Enterprise vendors (Corsearch, CSC, OpSec/Crane, MarkMonitor) sell online takedowns to large brands and none of their homepages mention customs; sub-$30M brands are not their customer. (2) Law firms treat recordation as a one-off filing, not a monitored program with an authentication desk; CBP asks for responses within 24 hours (https://www.cbp.gov/trade/priority-issues/ipr/bestpractices), so speed of response is the real product and it is an operations business. (3) Nobody found connects marketplace lookalike listings to bill-of-lading importers for small brands. Skeptical flags, most severe first: (1) Fee-sharing and unauthorized practice of law: a non-lawyer company taking 20-30% of settlements and receiving referral fees from IP counsel likely conflicts with ABA Model Rule 5.4-style bans on splitting fees with non-lawyers in most US states; get a legal opinion before fixing pricing. (2) CBP acts on counterfeit marks and recorded copyrights, not on look-alike dupes or trade-dress copies, so many indie-brand clones (copied design, no logo) are out of reach and the addressable pain is smaller than the pitch implies. (3) Importer identity: before seizure CBP typically does not give the trademark owner the importer name and address; unredacted images or samples come only after the importer gets notice and 7 business days to respond, and full importation details including importer name and address follow seizure within 30 business days (19 CFR 133.21, https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/19/133.21). BOL matching is the workaround, but public BOL data covers mostly ocean cargo, importers can request confidentiality (from memory, unverified), and much knockoff volume moves as parcels or via forwarders and non-resident importers. (4) Recordation needs a USPTO registration (about $350 per class) or a registered copyright, and many $1-30M brands lack full coverage. (5) The lever is $190 per class and the recordation, ID guide and training routes are free on cbp.gov, so the subscription must sell speed, labor and outcomes, not access. (6) Lever-rule (19 CFR 133.23, https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/19/133.23) covers gray-market goods that are physically and materially different; it does not address knockoffs and is a niche add-on.

result.white_space:
Research limits first. WebSearch hit its 200-call session cap before I could run any of the planned startup, Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt searches, so I did not verify the absence of a direct startup. I used WebFetch on named pages and GitHub repo searches instead. Wikipedia and vendor-site fetches turned up no company that recruits real, consenting individuals, enrols them in a platform's live ID or age-check flow, files deletion and access requests with the vendor and its sub-processors, watches for the canary strings, and issues an attestation. GitHub searches for open-source tools returned nothing relevant.

What is unserved: outcome-based, adversarial proof of the promise to forget. Incumbents cover the adjacent layers.
- Compliance automation (Vanta) covers whether controls exist on paper.
- Standards bodies (ACCS, Kantara, AVPA/ISO 27566) cover process and control audits.
- SecurityScorecard covers passive outside-in ratings.
- DSR orchestration (Transcend) covers a customer's own deletions.
- Honeytoken vendors cover a customer's own intrusions.
- HIBP-style monitors cover leaked-string detection.

The specific unserved piece is an independent, real-human, live-flow test with a public per-vendor retention benchmark.

Structural weaknesses of the pitch:
- Real government ID numbers cannot be unique canaries. Only emails, phones, addresses and name variants are. Leak detection depends on those fields surfacing in dumps, and image-only dumps are hard to search.
- The base rate of any given vendor leaking in a quarter is low. Most attestations would say nothing found, which is weak evidence. Retention and deletion behaviour, tested through DSARs and access requests, is the part canaries can actually prove.
- Vendors may treat the enrolments as terms-of-service violations. Customer consent helps but does not remove that risk.
- Privacy-preserving designs such as on-device age estimation and reusable digital ID could shrink the retention problem that this idea audits.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Indirect demand is strong. Direct demand is unproven: I found no customer, RFP or budget line for canary-based vendor testing.
- Vendor breaches are documented on Wikipedia's age-verification page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_verification_system). They are AU10TIX (2024), the Discord/Zendesk incident (2025), Persona (2026) and IDScan (2026, headlined as 150M+ driver's licences stolen). The Discord page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discord) says about 2.1M ID photos were claimed stolen and Discord says 70,000 users were affected. The AU10TIX page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AU10TIX) says its admin credentials were exposed online since 2022, that the company learned of it in 2024, and that it held international security certifications since 2020. The AU10TIX record backs the point that certified vendors still leak. I did not verify the IDScan details from a primary article, because the BleepingComputer URL I guessed returned 404.
- Regulator pressure is documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_Safety_Act_2023. Ofcom fines include £1M on AVS Group (Dec 2025), £50k on Itai Tech, and £20k plus £520k on 4chan. The Act's age-check deadline was 25 Jul 2025. That page has no guidance on platform liability for vendor data handling, so the pitch's claim that the platform owns its vendor's failure is not confirmed there.
- Compliance spend is real. Vanta reports about $300M ARR and 16,000+ customers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanta_(company)). That shows buyers pay for attestations but says nothing about paying for outcome testing.
- Not found: forum complaints from platforms about being unable to verify vendor deletion, cyber-insurer underwriting requirements for outcome testing, and pilot customers. The pitch's $25-100k per platform per vendor pricing is untested.
result.sharper_angle:
Narrow it to what canary humans can actually prove and sell it to the party that benefits most from independent proof.

1. Lead with deletion and access-request verification, not leak detection. Each canary files real deletion and access requests with the vendor and its sub-processors on a schedule, and the product measures whether they were honoured, how fast and with what residue. This is deterministic and repeatable, and it does not depend on a breach happening. Leak monitoring becomes a bonus signal instead of the headline claim.
2. Sell first to the vendors and to the certification ecosystem, not the platforms. ID and age-check vendors, AVPA and ACCS-audited providers and Ofcom-facing platforms all need independent evidence for sales and regulators. A vendor-commissioned, published retention-half-life attestation is sales collateral, as SOC 2 and ACCS marks are. That removes the ToS and consent problem, because the vendor consents. The platform-pays and insurer-pays tiers come later, as a buyer-commissioned unannounced audit.
3. Position it as the outcome layer that plugs into Vanta, SecurityScorecard, ACCS and Kantara, not a rival to them. Compliance tools ingest the attestation as evidence.
4. Publish the public per-vendor benchmark early, since none of the adjacent players has anything like it. Use it as the inbound engine and to build the insurer case.
5. Keep real people only, with unique emails, phones, addresses and name variants. Do not promise detection through government ID numbers, and state the detection limits honestly.
